author: AfricanFeminism
title: Liberia’s Feminist Foreign Policy: A Feminist Assertion of African Agency amid Global Backlash
content:
Liberia’s launch on 17 November 2026 of its 

Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy: A Feminist Foreign Policy

 is a continental milestone. The policy is rooted in Liberia’s anti-colonial legacy as Africa’s oldest republic and a founding voice in Pan-Africanism and multilateralism, an independent state that stood with the continent’s struggle for independence. That leadership, the policy recognises, has been carried forward in no small part by Liberian women. They are the long-standing custodians of this legacy, not new beneficiaries. The real test is whether the policy advances African agency on African terms amid a global backlash against gender equality, militarisation and democratic decline. The policy rests on five pillars, namely women’s rights; women, peace and security; women’s political representation and leadership; climate justice and natural resource governance; and women’s economic empowerment and inclusive trade.




The first pillar, women’s rights, builds on Liberia’s commitments under CEDAW, the Beijing Platform and the 

Maputo Protocol

. As anti-gender actors push a narrow “African values” framing of rights, credibility depends on Liberia practising at home what it champions abroad, including guaranteeing SRHR and protection from gender-based violence.

title: A Tribute to Veronica Lucy Gordon: South Sudan’s Courageous Voice for Women’s Rights and Press Freedom
content:
On 12 November 2026, Veronica Lucy Gordon, one of South Sudan’s pioneering journalists and most steadfast women’s rights activists, was shot dead in Western Equatoria province. She was on her way with friends to Mundri Town, taking part in the political life of a country on the brink. She was 

returning from party primaries

 and congress activities in Lui Payam in Mundri East County with eight  SPLM delegates when gunmen attacked their convoy at Miri Loko, killing Lucy and Justin Akim, a fellow party member and a delegate and leaving four delegates still missing. 




For more than forty years, Lucy was a formidable force through every phase of South Sudan’s struggle for self-determination. She worked alongside women, supporting their political ambitions—and was killed as she entered political leadership herself.




We met Lucy back in 2010, before South Sudan was born in 2011 and before the hopes of independence were dampened by the militarism and civil crisis that have taken so many lives. For several years, while we worked with the Women’s International Peace Centre, Lucy was our guiding light, making the work possible in an environment so difficult for women, both politically and culturally. title: Thirty Years On, Intersex Africans Set Their Own Agenda for Rights and Belonging
content:
It was a rare energy, fueled by our shared trials nd triumphs, and by stories that stretched beyond these walls. We, intersex activists from across Africa, came together, gathering on the shoulders of those who paved the way, held together by a promise that our voices would carry us far. Seeing the adoption of the Nairobi Declaration reminded me that our voices are now influencing regional conversations, policies and demands for justice.




We have come a long way. Years ago, people would laugh at you for raising intersex issues in Ghana; today, journalists call us to make documentaries.




On 26 October, we marked thirty years of Intersex Awareness Day. The day commemorates a 

1996 protest

 by intersex activists against unnecessary, irreversible surgeries on intersex children and their demand that we decide what happens to our own bodies. Thirty years on, that is still our demand: that we decide. Many gains since then have been won on this continent. South Africa’s equality law has recognised intersex status since 2005. Kenya became the first African country to 

count intersex people in a census

 in 2019, and its 

Children Act 2022

title: Eight Years in Prison for Fighting Anti-Black Racism in Tunisia: Free Saadia Mosbah!
content:
For years, Saadia Mosbah has been one of the leading voices against anti-Black racism in Tunisia. As president of the anti-racism organisation Mnemty, she has stood up for Black Tunisians and Black migrants alike. When

 

violence against Black migrants escalated

 after President Kais Saied’s February 2023 statement against African migrants, she became a target of online hate campaigns.




On May 6, 2024, she was arrested. On March 19, 2026, she was sentenced to eight years in prison and a heavy fine on charges of money laundering and illicit enrichment. On June 23, the Tunis Court of Appeals upheld her conviction, along with those of five Mnemty colleagues and associates. A final appeal, filed on June 29, is now before the Court of Cassation.




Human rights movements and organisations,

 

including Amnesty International

, have denounced the irregularities in the proceedings and the lack of evidence for the alleged offences. They have also raised the alarm over the racist treatment and violence Saadia has reportedly suffered in detention.
